items.title: Lecture: Loss Aversion in Behavioural Finance

lines.t: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at one of the most robust findings in behavioural finance, namely loss aversion.
Put simply, loss aversion is the tendency for people to feel the pain of a loss more intensely than the pleasure of an equivalent gain.
Experimental studies suggest that, for many people, a loss feels roughly twice as powerful as a gain of the same size.
Now, why does this matter for investors? Well, consider what's known as the disposition effect.
Investors tend to sell shares that have risen in value too early, in order to lock in a gain, while holding on to shares that have fallen, hoping they'll recover.
From a purely rational perspective, the price you originally paid is irrelevant. What matters is the expected future return of each investment.
But psychologically, selling a losing position means admitting the loss, turning a paper loss into a real one, and that is precisely what loss-averse investors try to avoid.
I should stress that loss aversion is not irrational in every context. In environments where losses can be catastrophic, caution may well be adaptive.
For next week, I'd like you to read the chapter on framing effects and think about how the same choice can be presented as either a gain or a loss.

items.title: Interview for a Financial Analyst Role

lines.t: Thanks for coming in. Could you tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a senior stakeholder?
Sure. In my last role, I discovered that a revenue forecast our team had already presented to the CFO was overstated by about fifteen per cent.
The error came from a currency assumption that hadn't been updated. It wasn't my model, but I was the one who spotted it.
How did you handle it?
First, I double-checked the numbers with a colleague, because I wanted to be absolutely sure before raising the alarm.
Then I asked my manager if we could brief the CFO together that same afternoon, rather than waiting for the monthly review.
We went in with the corrected figures, a clear explanation of what had gone wrong, and a proposal to add an automated check on exchange rates.
And how did the CFO react?
She wasn't thrilled, obviously, but she said she appreciated hearing it from us first. The automated check is still in use, as far as I know.

items.title: News Bulletin: Housing Starts and Rates

lines.t: Housing starts fell sharply last month, according to new figures, as higher borrowing costs continued to weigh on the construction sector. Our business correspondent has more.
Construction began on just under two hundred thousand homes on an annualised basis, down nine per cent from the previous month and well below what economists had forecast.
The slowdown was concentrated in multi-unit buildings such as condominiums, where developers say rising financing costs have made many projects unviable.
The figures will add to pressure on governments, which have pledged to dramatically increase housing supply to address chronic affordability problems.
Industry groups are calling for faster permit approvals and lower development charges, arguing that red tape adds months and tens of thousands of dollars to every project.
Some economists, however, caution against reading too much into a single month's data, noting that housing starts are notoriously volatile.
Thank you. In other business news, the dollar edged higher against its US counterpart this afternoon.

items.title: Podcast: Will AI Change How We Learn at Work?

lines.t: My guest today has spent the last decade studying how organisations train their people. Welcome to the show.
Thanks for having me. It's a topic that's gone from niche to front-page news in about eighteen months.
So let me put the provocative version to you first. If an AI assistant can answer any question instantly, why bother learning anything at all?
It's a fair question, but I think it rests on a misunderstanding of what expertise is. Expertise isn't a stock of answers; it's the ability to recognise which questions are worth asking.
A junior analyst with a brilliant tool will still struggle if they can't tell when the output is subtly wrong. And the only way to develop that judgement is, frankly, to have done the work yourself.
But isn't there a risk that companies cut the very entry-level tasks through which people used to develop that judgement?
That, to my mind, is the real danger, far more than mass unemployment. If the apprenticeship layer disappears, where does the next generation of experts come from?
The more forward-thinking firms are redesigning roles so that juniors still wrestle with problems, but with an AI acting more like a demanding tutor than a ghostwriter.
A demanding tutor rather than a ghostwriter. I like that. We'll pick that thread up after the break.

items.title: Panel: Can Growth and Climate Goals Coexist?

lines.t: Our question tonight: can economies keep growing while cutting emissions fast enough to meet climate targets?
The evidence suggests they can, at least partially. Over thirty countries have grown their economies while reducing emissions, which we call absolute decoupling.
With respect, the pace matters. Decoupling is happening, but nowhere near quickly enough. At current rates, we'd overshoot our targets by decades.
I don't dispute that. My point is that growth itself isn't the enemy. What matters is what we grow: renewable energy, efficient buildings, public transport.
But there's a risk that green growth becomes an excuse for business as usual, as if technology will rescue us without any change in how we consume.
So is there any common ground?
Plenty, I'd say. We both want a much higher carbon price and far faster investment in clean infrastructure.
Agreed. Where we differ is on whether rich countries should also aim to consume less. I believe they should.

items.title: Radio Talk: The Ethics of Nudging

lines.t: A nudge, in the jargon of behavioural economics, is any feature of the way a choice is presented that predictably alters behaviour without forbidding any option or significantly changing incentives.

Placing fruit at eye level in a canteen is a nudge; banning chips is not. Automatically enrolling employees in a pension scheme, while allowing them to opt out, is perhaps the best-known example, and it has dramatically increased saving rates.
Proponents describe this as libertarian paternalism: steering people towards choices they would endorse on reflection, while leaving them free to choose otherwise.
Critics are unconvinced. If nudges work precisely because people do not notice them, the objection goes, they bypass rather than respect our capacity for reason.
There is also the awkward question of who decides which direction we are nudged in, and on what authority. A nudge towards saving seems benign; a nudge towards a particular political view would not.

My own view is that the defence of nudging depends heavily on transparency. A nudge that would still work if it were openly disclosed is, I think, far easier to justify than one that relies on our not knowing it is there.
